To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) relativistic canonical velocity distribution functions may be obtained as solutions of relative entropy problems; (ii) the Juttner distribution, which is the most frequently used relativistic velocity distribution, is the solution of a relative entropy problem with respect to an (additive) reference measure that is invariant under translations on momentum space; (iii) a modified Juttner distribution may be derived by requiring Lorentz invari- ance of the reference measure.

(i) the BGS entropy, which is the most commonly used entropy in physics, is a special case relative entropy; (ii) the standard Juttmer distribution is related to a reference measure which is invariant under additive translation of momenta; (iii) the modified Juttmer distribution results from imposing invariance under Lorentz transformations of the reference measure.
(i) The standard Juttner velocity distribution is a solution of the maximum entropy principle with respect to a reference measure which is invariant under translations on momentum space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how to identify the reference measure for a given group of transformations.
a new interpretation of the thermodynamic maximum entropy principle, which may provide a better understanding of the underlying physics.
the question how the choice of a reference measure influences the form of a canonical distribution and the associated thermodynamic equilibrium state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the standard Jüttner distribution is a canonical velocity distribution with respect to the translation group, while the modified Juttner distribution can be considered a canonical velocity distribution in terms of the Lorentz group.
the maximum BGS-entropy principle is a useful tool to identify equilibrium distributions in the context of relativistic statistical mechanics.

the Juttner distribution describes the equilibrium velocity distribution of a gas of relativistic, non-interacting particles, if and only if the reference measure is invariant with respect to translations on momentum space.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for relativistic particles, the BGS entropy may be considered as a special case of the relative entropy, which is related to a reference measure on momentum space that is invariant under the Lorentz group.
the BGS maximum entropy principle is a useful tool for the characterization of equilibrium states, if the underlying reference measure exhibits the desired transformation properties.

the maximum entropy problem for the Boltzann–Gibbs-Shannon entropy is a special instance of relative entropy maximization, where the reference measure is invariant under the action of an additive group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BGS-entropy maximum principle can be understood as an optimization problem with respect to an underlying reference measure.
, in contrast to non-relativistic kinetic theory, the choice of the underlying reference measures is not unique.
the maximum entropy principle is not only applicable to equilibrium systems, but can also be applied in the study of nonequilibrium phenomena.
